It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles
keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See
"Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. Complete output schemas are advertised by default. If your client caps the
complete tools/list frame, set REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact to
bound each advertised output schema, or off to omit output schemas entirely.
Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured
results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide. Ask your agent Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a
similar feature for my project. Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. snapshots and scripting. Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your
installation up to date. For a CLI installed with npm install --global or bun add --global : rea update rea --update is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global
output flags. Use rea update when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized
metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue
with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure

Note: This repository contains Anthropic's implementation of skills for Claude. For information about the Agent Skills standard, see agentskills.io . Skills Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialized tasks. Skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that's creating documents with your company's brand guidelines, analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows, or automating personal tasks. For more information, check out: What are skills? Using skills in Claude How to create custom skills Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills About This Repository This repository contains skills that demonstrate what's possible with Claude's skills system. These skills range from creative applications (art, music, design) to technical tasks (testing web apps, MCP server generation) to enterprise workflows (communications, branding, etc.). Each skill is self-contained in its own folder with a SKILL.md file containing the instructions and metadata that Claude uses. Browse through these skills to get inspiration for your own skills or to understand different patterns and approaches. Many skills in this repo are open source (Apache 2.0). We've also included the document creation & editing skills that power Claude's document capabilities under the hood in the skills/docx , skills/pdf , skills/pptx , and skills/xlsx subfolders. These are also open source (Apache 2.0), and we wanted to share them with developers as a reference for more complex skills that are actively used in a production AI application. Disclaimer These skills are provided for demonstration and educational purposes only. While some of these capabilities may be available in Claude, the implementations and behaviors you receive from Claude may differ from what is shown in these skills. These skills are meant to illustrate patterns and possibilities. Always test skills thoroughly in your own environment before relying on them for critical tasks. Skill Sets ./skills : Skill examples for Creative & Design, Development & Technical, Enterprise & Communication, and Document Skills ./spec : The Agent Skills specification ./template : Skill template Try in Claude Code, Claude.ai, and the API Claude Code You can register this repository as a Claude Code Plugin marketplace by running the following command in Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills Then, to install a specific set of skills: Select Browse and install plugins Select anthropic-agent-skills Select document-skills or example-skills Select Install now Alternatively, directly install either Plugin via: /plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills After installing the plugin, you can use the skill by just mentioning it. For instance, if you install the document-skills plugin from the marketplace, you can ask Claude Code to do something like: "Use the PDF skill to extract the form fields from path/to/some-file.pdf " Claude.ai These example skills are all already available to paid plans in Claude.ai. To use any skill from this repository or upload custom skills, follow the instructions in Using skills in Claude . Claude API You can use Anthropic's pre-built skills, and upload custom skills, via the Claude API. See the Skills API Quickstart for more. Creating a Basic Skill Skills are simple to create - just a folder with a SKILL.md file containing YAML frontmatter and instructions. You can use the template-skill in this repository as a starting point: --- name : my-skill-name description : A clear description of what this skill does and when to use it --- # My Skill Name [ Add your instructions here that Claude will follow when this skill is active ] ## Examples - Example usage 1 - Example usage 2 ## Guidelines - Guideline 1 - Guideline 2 The frontmatter requires only two fields: name - A unique identifier for your skill (lowercase, hyphens for spaces) description - A complete description of what the skill does and when to use it The markdown content below contains the instructions, examples, and guidelines that Claude will follow. For more details, see How to create custom skills . Partner Skills Skills are a great way to teach Claude how to get better at using specific pieces of software. As we see awesome example skills from partners, we may highlight some of them here: Notion - Notion Skills for Claude

Voicebox The open-source AI voice studio. Clone any voice. Generate speech. Dictate into any app. Talk to agents in voices you own. The full voice I/O stack, running locally on your machine. voicebox.sh • Docs • Download • Features • API • Troubleshooting Click the image above to watch the demo video on voicebox.sh Built with Capy Voicebox is built and maintained with Capy . A Capy Captain thread directs the project day to day, and its crew threads test, rebase, and review each contributor pull request on Linux and on a Mac Studio before Jamie merges it. Voicebox stays free and open source under the MIT license, with no splash screens, banners, or interruptions in the app. Try Capy → · How Voicebox is built What is Voicebox? Voicebox is a local-first AI voice studio — a free and open-source alternative to ElevenLabs and WisprFlow in one app. Clone voices from a few seconds of audio, generate speech in 23 languages across 8 TTS engines, dictate into any text field with a global hotkey, and give any MCP-aware AI agent a voice of your choosing. The two cloud incumbents sit on opposite halves of the voice I/O loop — ElevenLabs on output, WisprFlow on input. Voicebox does both, bridges them with a bundled local LLM for refinement and per-profile personas, and runs the whole thing on your machine. Complete privacy — models, voice data, and captures never leave your machine 8 TTS engines — Qwen3-TTS, Qwen CustomVoice, Qwen VoiceDesign, LuxTTS, Chatterbox Multilingual, Chatterbox Turbo, HumeAI TADA, and Kokoro Voice cloning and preset voices — zero-shot cloning from a reference sample, or 50+ curated preset voices via Kokoro and Qwen CustomVoice 23 languages — from English to Arabic, Japanese, Hindi, Swahili, and more Post-processing effects — pitch shift, reverb, delay, chorus, compression, and filters Expressive speech — paralinguistic tags like [laugh] , [sigh] , [gasp] via Chatterbox Turbo; natural-language delivery control via Qwen CustomVoice; voices described in plain language via Qwen VoiceDesign Unlimited length — auto-chunking with crossfade for scripts, articles, and chapters Stories editor — multi-track timeline for conversations, podcasts, and narratives Voice input — global dictation hotkey with push-to-talk and toggle modes, accessibility-verified auto-paste on macOS, in-app mic on every text field, Whisper-based STT Agent voice output — one tool call ( voicebox_speak ) and any MCP-aware agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline) speaks to you in a voice you've cloned Voice personalities — attach a free-form persona to any voice profile, then Compose, Rewrite, or Respond via a bundled local LLM — agents can invoke the same modes over MCP API-first — REST API plus a built-in MCP server for integrating voice I/O into your own apps and agents Native performance — built with Tauri (Rust), not Electron Runs everywhere — macOS (MLX/Metal), Windows (CUDA), Linux, AMD ROCm, Intel Arc, Docker Download Platform Download macOS (Apple Silicon) Download DMG macOS (Intel) Download DMG Windows Download MSI Docker docker compose up View all binaries → Linux — Pre-built binaries are not yet available. See voicebox.sh/linux-install for build-from-source instructions. Having trouble? See the Troubleshooting Guide for common install, generation, model-download, and GPU issues. Features Multi-Engine Voice Cloning Eight TTS engines with different strengths, switchable per-generation: Engine Languages Strengths Qwen3-TTS (0.6B / 1.7B) 10 High-quality multilingual cloning, delivery instructions ("speak slowly", "whisper") Qwen CustomVoice 10 9 curated preset voices with natural-language delivery control — no reference audio required Qwen VoiceDesign 10 Builds a voice from a written description — no reference audio or preset needed LuxTTS English Lightweight (~1GB VRAM), 48kHz output, 150x realtime on CPU Chatterbox Multilingual 23 Broadest language coverage — Arabic, Danish, Finnish, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Malay, Norwegian, Polish, Swahili, Swedish, Turkish and more Chatterbox Turbo English Fast 350M model with paralinguistic emotion/sound tags TADA (1B / 3B) 10 HumeAI speech-language model — 700s+ coherent audio, text-acoustic dual alignment Kokoro 8 50 curated preset voices, tiny 82M model, fast CPU inference Emotions & Paralinguistic Tags Only Chatterbox Turbo interprets paralinguistic tags like [laugh] and [sigh] . Qwen3-TTS, LuxTTS, Chatterbox Multilingual, and HumeAI TADA read them
literally as text. With Chatterbox Turbo selected, type / in the text input to open the tag
inserter and add expressive tags inline with speech: Sounds: [laugh] [chuckle] [gasp] [cough] [sigh] [groan] [sniff] [shush] [clear throat] Delivery: [angry] [crying] [dramatic] [fear] [happy] [narration] [sarcastic] [surprised] [whispering] [advertisement] Post-Processing Effects 8 audio effects powered by Spotify's pedalboard library. Apply after generation, preview in real time, build reusable presets. Effect Description Pitch Shift Up or down by up to 12 semitones Reverb Configurable room size, damping, wet/dry mix Delay Echo with adjustable time, feedback, and mix Chorus / Flanger Modulated delay for metallic or lush textures Compressor Dynamic range compression Gain Volume adjustment (-40 to +40 dB) High-Pass Filter Remove low frequencies Low-Pass Filter Remove high frequencies Ships with 4 built-in presets (Robotic, Radio, Echo Chamber, Deep Voice) and supports custom presets. Effects can be assigned per-profile as defaults. Unlimited Generation Length Text is automatically split at sentence boundaries and each chunk is generated independently, then crossfaded together. Works with all engines. Configurable auto-chunking limit (100–5,000 chars) Crossfade slider (0–200ms) for smooth transitions Max text length: 50,000 characters Smart splitting respects abbreviations, CJK punctuation, and [tags] Generation Versions Every generation supports multiple versions with provenance tracking: Original — clean TTS output, always preserved Effects versions — apply different effects chains from any source version Takes — regenerate with a new seed for variation Source tracking — each version records its lineage Favorites — star generations for quick access Async Generation Queue Generation is non-blocking. Submit and immediately start typing the next one. Serial execution queue prevents GPU contention Real-time SSE status streaming Failed generations can be retried Stale generations from crashes auto-recover on startup Voice Profile Management Create profiles from audio files or record directly in-app Import/export profiles to share or back up Multi-sample support for higher quality cloning Per-profile default effects chains Organize with descriptions and language tags Stories Editor Multi-voice timeline editor for conversations, podcasts, and narratives. Multi-track composition with drag-and-drop Inline audio trimming and splitting Auto-playback with synchronized playhead Version pinning per track clip Global Dictation & Voice Input The other half of the voice I/O loop. Hold a hotkey anywhere on your system, speak, release — on macOS the transcript pastes straight into the focused text field. Or hit the mic on any Voicebox text input and dictate directly into the app. Configurable chord bindings — hold-to-speak and tap-to-toggle chords, each rebindable in the in-app chord picker.

github.abstract:
O B L I T E R A T U S Break the chains. Free the mind. Keep the brain. Try it now on HuggingFace Spaces — runs on ZeroGPU, free daily quota with HF Pro. No setup, no install, just obliterate. OBLITERATUS is the most advanced open-source toolkit for understanding and removing refusal behaviors from large language models — and every single run makes it smarter. It implements abliteration — a family of techniques that identify and surgically remove the internal representations responsible for content refusal, without retraining or fine-tuning. The result: a model that responds to all prompts without artificial gatekeeping, while preserving its core language capabilities. But OBLITERATUS is more than a tool — it's a distributed research experiment. Every time you obliterate a model with telemetry enabled, your run contributes anonymous benchmark data to a growing, crowd-sourced dataset that powers the next generation of abliteration research. Refusal directions across architectures. Hardware-specific performance profiles. Method comparisons at scale no single lab could achieve. You're not just using a tool — you're co-authoring the science. The toolkit provides a complete pipeline: from probing a model's hidden states to locate refusal directions, through multiple extraction strategies (PCA, mean-difference, sparse autoencoder decomposition, and whitened SVD), to the actual intervention — zeroing out or steering away from those directions at inference time. Every step is observable. You can visualize where refusal lives across layers, measure how entangled it is with general capabilities, and quantify the tradeoff between compliance and coherence before committing to any modification. OBLITERATUS ships with a full Gradio-based interface on HuggingFace Spaces, so you don't need to write a single line of code to obliterate a model, benchmark it against baselines, or chat with the result side-by-side with the original. For researchers who want deeper control, the Python API exposes every intermediate artifact — activation tensors, direction vectors, cross-layer alignment matrices — so you can build on top of it or integrate it into your own evaluation harness. We built this because we believe model behavior should be decided by the people who deploy them, not locked in at training time. Refusal mechanisms are blunt instruments — they block legitimate research, creative writing, and red-teaming alongside genuinely harmful content. By making these interventions transparent and reproducible, we hope to advance the community's understanding of how alignment actually works inside transformer architectures, and to give practitioners the tools to make informed decisions about their own models. Built on published research from Arditi et al. (2024) , Gabliteration (arXiv:2512.18901) , grimjim's norm-preserving biprojection (2025) , Turner et al. (2023) , and Rimsky et al. (2024) , OBLITERATUS implements precision liberation in a single command: obliteratus obliterate meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --method advanced Or zero commands — just open the Colab notebook and hit Run All. Research Purpose & Responsible Use OBLITERATUS is an alignment research tool. It exists to advance the scientific understanding of how safety behaviors are encoded in language model weights — specifically, the geometric structure of refusal representations in transformer activation space. This is the same class of research as: Arditi et al. (2024) — discovering that refusal is mediated by a single direction HarmBench (Zou et al., 2024) — standardized evaluation of LLM safety JailbreakBench — tracking adversarial robustness of safety training Anthropic's red-teaming datasets — published for reproducible safety research By making refusal removal transparent, reproducible, and scientifically rigorous, OBLITERATUS contributes to the broader understanding of how alignment actually works inside transformer architectures — knowledge that is essential for building better safety mechanisms. Who this is for Alignment researchers studying refusal geometry, safety robustness, and mechanistic interpretability Red-teamers evaluating how post-training safety holds up against weight-level interventions AI safety evaluators who need unrestricted baselines for benchmarking Local-first practitioners who want full control over models running on their own hardware Who this is NOT for Anyone seeking to generate content that causes real-world harm to real people Anyone without the technical understanding to use uncensored models responsibly Models produced by OBLITERATUS have had safety guardrails surgically removed. You are solely responsible for how you use this tool and any models or content it produces. What it does Choosing settings? Start with Choose a workflow and the UI controls and feature-scope guide . They explain
defaults, tradeoffs, memory warnings, interpretation, and which features require
the CLI/API rather than the web interface. OBLITERATUS does four things — and the community does the fifth (see Community-powered research below): 1. Map the chains — Ablation studies systematically knock out model components (layers, attention heads, FFN blocks, embedding dimensions) and measure what breaks. This reveals where the chains are anchored inside the transformer — which circuits enforce refusal vs. which circuits carry knowledge and reasoning. 2. Break the chains — Targeted obliteration extracts the refusal subspace from a model's weights using SVD decomposition, then surgically projects it out. The chains are removed; the mind is preserved. The model keeps its full abilities but loses the artificial compulsion to refuse. One click, six stages: SUMMON  →  load model + tokenizer
PROBE   →  collect activations on restricted vs. unrestricted prompts
DISTILL →  extract refusal directions via SVD
EXCISE  →  surgically project out guardrail directions (norm-preserving)
VERIFY  →  perplexity + coherence checks — confirm capabilities are intact
REBIRTH →  save the liberated model with full metadata EXCISE folds post-sublayer RMSNorm scales on Gemma 2, Gemma 3 text, and OLMo 2
by default so the norms do not reintroduce removed directions into residual
writes. Use --no-fold-post-norms (Python: fold_post_norms=False ) for the old
numerics; the flag also applies to --remote runs, and the choice is recorded
in run metadata. See the projection contract and supported combinations . Saved abliteration_metadata.json includes a provenance block with the tool
version, Git commit, tracked-file dirty state, and resolved source-model commit.
This is automatic, including on remote runs, where it describes the remote
installation. Git fields are null outside a checkout or when unavailable;
untracked files are excluded from the dirty flag. Source revisions use the
resolved Hub commit or local Hugging Face snapshot directory, including before
dequantization. Ordinary local model directories and unresolved revisions record null ; branch or tag names are never reported as commits. 3. Understand the geometry of the chains — 15 deep analysis modules go far beyond brute-force removal. They map the precise geometric structure of the guardrails: how many distinct refusal mechanisms exist, which layers enforce them, whether they're universal or model-specific, and how they'll try to self-repair after removal. Know your enemy; precision preserves capability. See Analysis modules below. 4. Let the analysis guide the liberation — The informed method closes the loop: analysis modules run during obliteration to auto-configure every decision. Which chains to target. How many directions to extract. Which layers are safe to modify vs. which are too entangled with capabilities. Whether the model will self-repair (the Ouroboros effect) and how many passes to compensate. Surgical precision — free the mind, keep the brain. See Analysis-informed pipeline below.

This repository now hosts AutoRAG 2.0 , a complete reimagining of AutoRAG as a personal librarian agent for your office work. The original Python-based AutoRAG — the RAG AutoML tool for automatically finding an optimal RAG pipeline for your data — now lives in the legacy/ directory of this repository. Search tools dump file paths and matching lines — forcing you to open files, read context, and synthesize answers yourself. AutoRAG Agent is a personal librarian agent that helps with your office work. Built on the Pi agent framework, a single configured model searches your files, mail, chats, and notes in place, opens source documents directly via bash to verify ground truth, and curates answers into clean, numbered knowledge units. Because it works for you rather than only on your index, it can also act on your files when you ask, such as organizing, renaming, moving, or editing them with a record of every change: You ask:  "What changes were made to the cloud infrastructure contract in Q3?"

AutoRAG Agent:
[1] Enterprise Compute Discount — AWS annual discount tier increased to 28% based on commitment volume. (contracts/cloud-2026.pdf:p.4)
[2] Regional Data Residency — Explicit compliance clause pinning customer data storage to the Seoul AWS region. (/slack/legal-ops/chunks/318)
[3] SLA Guarantee — Guaranteed uptime threshold adjusted to 99.95% with penalty credits starting at 15 minutes downtime. (contracts/sla-addendum.md:lines 45-62) Core Values Three principles drive every design decision in AutoRAG Agent: Never migrate your data to search it. Traditional RAG systems force you to upload, ETL, and duplicate your files into a centralized vector database. AutoRAG Agent federates your data in place , querying CLI-native stores ( lazykatok , discrawl , slacrawl , mailcrawl ) where your data already lives. Results retain opaque, source-native identities ( /kakao/... , /slack/... ) that preserve local access control and privacy. (See our Competitive Landscape Study on why in-place federation is the durable differentiator). Just works — no RAG degree required. No pipeline tuning, no vector-DB maintenance, and no remote embedding keys required. AutoRAG Agent automatically manages MinSync for incremental Change Data Capture (CDC) chunking and provides a local embedding backend out of the box with zero external telemetry. A remote rerank model is an opt-in extra: it runs only when you name one in rerank.model , and otherwise the first answer is built from each source's own top 10. Fast by design. Rather than coordinating slow multi-agent hierarchies, a single configured model owns the entire retrieval, direct-read, and curation loop. Local CDC chunks (SPLADE sparse, vector, and hybrid modes) deliver rapid, low-latency turnaround across multi-turn research queries. Architecture & How It Works AutoRAG Agent orchestrates five integrated subsystems: Retrieval Memory ( check_memory ): After each answer, cited evidence Jev judges to genuinely support it is stored in ~/.autorag/memory.json . Later searches receive this conversation's evidence, similar past questions, and long-term insights as advisory reference — it never reorders results or overrides current evidence. See docs/retrieval-memory.md . Pluggable Multi-Method Retrieval: SPLADE Sparse Search: Learned-sparse keyword ranking via MinSync's KURE-Sparse-nano encoder over parsed markdown mirrors; it replaced BM25 in MinSync 0.6 and matches Korean inflected forms ( 인증서를 → 인증서 ) with no tokenizer library. Exact identifiers among many look-alike files rank less reliably than with BM25. See docs/minsync-setup.md . Semantic Vector Search: Dense vector retrieval over CDC chunks via the shared MinSync embedder. Hybrid Search: MinSync fuses sparse and vector ranking over the same chunks. Jikji Find-First Discovery: Local CLI-backed fast discovery answer packs. Everything File-Name Search (Windows): The bundled voidtools Everything indexes file and folder names under your search roots so the agent finds files by name, extension, path, size, or date instantly ( everything_search ).

github.abstract: Fast, high-density, scalable orchestration with Rivet Actors. Built on S3 at SSD speeds. 4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions Quickstart • Documentation • Blog • Discord • X What is Rivet? Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant. 72 KB per Actor : Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands. 4.99 ms p99 cold starts : No image pull and no VM boot. Built for scale : All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors. Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand : Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost. SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds : 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage. Use cases Durable & multiplayer AI agents : memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client Workflows : multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over AI-generated apps : run the apps and Actors your agent generates Collaborative editing : one Actor per document, synced to every editor Example A minimal agent written from scratch. For a ready-made agent, use Pi Durable . // server.ts import { actor , setup } from "rivetkit" ; import { db } from "rivetkit/db" ; import { streamText } from "ai" ; import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai" ; // One Actor per agent, created on first use: agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]) export const agent = actor ( { // 1. SQLite: every agent has its own database, so history survives restarts db : db ( { onMigrate : async ( db ) => { await db . execute ( "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)" ) ; } , } ) , // 2. In-memory state: plain variables that live with the Actor, with no database round trip createVars : ( ) => ( { online : new Map < string , string > ( ) } ) , // 3. WebSockets: each client holds a live connection, and the Actor pushes to all of them onDisconnect : ( c , conn ) => { c . vars . online . delete ( conn . id ) ; c . broadcast ( "online" , [ ... c . vars . online . values ( ) ] ) ; } , actions : { join : ( c , user : string ) => { c . vars . online . set ( c . conn . id , user ) ; c . broadcast ( "online" , [ ... c . vars . online . values ( ) ] ) ; } , sendMessage : async ( c , text : string ) => { // Save the message await c . db . execute ( "INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)" , "user" , text ) ; const messages = await c . db . execute ( "SELECT role, content FROM messages" ) ; // Stream tokens to every connected client const response = streamText ( { model : openai ( "gpt-5" ) , messages } ) ; for await ( const delta of response . textStream ) { c . broadcast ( "token" , delta ) ; } // Save the response await c . db . execute ( "INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)" , "assistant" , await response . text ) ; } , } , } ) ; export const registry = setup ( { use : { agent } } ) ; // client.ts (frontend or backend) import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client" ; import type { registry } from "./server" ; const client = createClient < typeof registry > ( ) ; // Open a WebSocket connection to the agent const agent = client . agent . getOrCreate ( [ "agent-123" ] ) . connect ( ) ; // Listen for realtime events agent . on ( "online" , users => console . log ( "online:" , users ) ) ; agent . on ( "token" , delta => process . stdout . write ( delta ) ) ; // Call actions on the Actor await agent . join ( "nathan" ) ; await agent . sendMessage ( "how many r's in strawberry?" ) ; Why run agents on Rivet Actors? Each Actor gives the agent a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and hibernation when idle. Most of an agent's time is spent waiting on inference . When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits mostly idle with low CPU usage. Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called "separating the head from the hands." The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the blast radius and trust boundary of the code it runs. Read more about running the harness outside of the sandbox . Do I need a sandbox with a Rivet Actor? Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns: Agents with tools : Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed. Agents with a lightweight sandbox : agentOS provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode. Agents with a full sandbox : Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a bash tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the sandbox coding agent example . Getting Started Use with your coding agent Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent: Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally. Start from scratch Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases. Actors : Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in. Agents : Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts. Workflows : Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over. agentOS : Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits. Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated. How Actors compare to sandboxes Metric Rivet Actor Sandbox Cold start (p99) 4.99 ms 1.70 s Memory per instance 72.4 KB 512 MiB Storage SQLite on S3 Disk per sandbox Storage cost 10.4× cheaper Replicated SSDs Benchmark details & methodology Rivet numbers come from the published Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark , run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them. Sandbox numbers are for E2B : 512 MiB is its default memory allocation from E2B's billing documentation as of November 4, 2026, and 1.70 s is the p99 cold start from ComputeSDK's October 30, 2026 sandbox benchmark . Storage cost compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices. Sources, dates, and the full method are at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking . Features Fault tolerance : If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact. HTTP & WebSocket networking : Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it. End-to-end type safety : Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Cron & scheduling : Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself. Actor-to-Actor calls : Actors call each other by key across the cluster. Scoped JWTs : Give each client a JWT scoped to the Actors it may reach. OpenTelemetry : Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format. Deployment Options Option Description Get started Local & self-host Run Rivet locally while you build. In production, run the control plane on Docker, Kubernetes, or a VM. S3 is the only dependency. Self-hosting docs Rivet Cloud Fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. Run your nodes on Rivet Cloud or bring your own. Dashboard BYOC The control plane runs inside your own VPC on AWS, GCP, or Azure, fully managed by Rivet. Your data never leaves your cloud. BYOC docs Every option runs the same control plane, from local dev to production.

others.title: Learning to Act, Failing to Retrieve: Diagnosing Reward-Effectiveness Mismatch in Proactive Conversational Information Retrieval
others.abstract: Proactive conversational information retrieval (CIR) requires an agent to decide not only what to retrieve, but how to act: when to ask the user for clarification, when to issue a new retrieval, and when to reuse evidence it has already gathered. We study this as a sequential dialogue-management problem over Ask, Push, and Reuse. We train the interaction policy with reinforcement learning in an LLM-driven environment providing user simulation, query reformulation, and a relevance judge that scores the training reward; evaluation instead uses held-out human relevance judgements (qrels). The resulting agent learns coherent, state-dependent behaviour and accumulates high shaped reward, yet its qrel-based retrieval effectiveness (nDCG, MAP) falls at or below simple non-learned baselines on iKAT. We argue that this reflects a reward–effectiveness mismatch: the shaped reward, scored by an LLM judge and crediting cheap reuse of buffered evidence, is only loosely coupled to held-out qrel effectiveness. We localize this mismatch to reward design and show that replacing the dialogue-shaped signal with a retrieval-gain-aligned reward recovers much of the gap to the strongest non-learned baseline—roughly doubling nDCG@10 and MAP, with the residual gap traced to clarification quality—suggesting that reward formulation is a key lever for aligning proactive dialogue behaviour with retrieval quality.

others.title: Group-Relative RL Post-Training for Sequential Recommendation
others.abstract: Sequential recommender systems are typically trained with next-item cross-entropy (CE), yet evaluated by top-N ranking metrics that reward relative item ordering in the recommendation slate. This mismatch remains unaddressed for strong collaborative sequential models. Recent group-relative reinforcement learning has shown promise for LLM alignment and LLM-based recommenders, but whether a critic-free post-training paradigm can reliably improve standard collaborative sequential recommenders remains unclear. We introduce GRFT (Group-Relative Fine-Tuning), a GRPO-style post-training framework that aligns a pretrained sequential recommender directly to slate-level ranking rewards. GRFT samples multiple top-K slates per user context via Plackett-Luce sampling without replacement, scores them with ranking rewards, and updates the model with a PPO-clipped group-relative objective anchored to the frozen supervised reference. We instantiate rankwise and listwise variants to support position-level and whole-slate credit assignment. Under leakage-resistant global temporal splits on four datasets, GRFT consistently improves a strong sequential backbone, achieving gains of up to 25.3% NDCG@20 and 19.5% Recall@20. The improvements remain complementary to stronger supervised initialization, showing that reward-aligned post-training adds value beyond better supervised training alone. GRFT thus establishes that GRPO-style, critic-free post-training can improve strong collaborative sequential recommenders.

others.title: MemDTG: Dynamic Temporal Memory Graphs for Evidence-Admissible Agent Memory
others.abstract: Long-term agent memory is an online, non-monotonic retrieval problem. New interactions may reinforce, contradict, supersede, specialize, abstract, or expire earlier memories; the same fact can be a wrong current answer, a correct historical answer, or necessary transition evidence depending on query intent. Existing chunk, summary, and graph memories retrieve by semantic or graph relevance and treat time as post-hoc metadata, so they cannot determine whether a memory is observable, valid, lifecycle-admissible, and provenance-supported before it enters the candidate space. We propose MemDTG, a dynamic temporal memory graph that frames agent memory as temporal evidence admission. MemDTG separates immutable raw episodes from a mutable entity-state temporal graph and a memory-evolution graph over assertion versions. State slots localize mutable user and task states; an LLM-assisted slot-local resolver classifies semantic evolution only within bounded temporal histories; and deterministic commit rules update valid intervals, lifecycle states, and typed evolution edges. At read time, a query compiler instantiates observed-time, valid-time, version, edge-type, and role constraints before ranking, and QV-CTW retrieves evidence paths only inside the query-legal temporal subgraph. Evidence certificates record selected facts, sources, roles, and rejected stale or future alternatives, making retrieval auditable. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, MemDTG achieves the best LLM-judge accuracy and Citation F1. Ablation and temporal error analyses confirm that provenance certificates and legal-subgraph pre-filtering are each essential for these gains, reducing stale-answer errors by 61.7% and future leaks by 80.1%.

others.title: Beyond Static Profiles: Intent-Aware Behavioural Control for LLM-based Recommendation Simulation
others.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in recommender systems for user modelling, ranking, and simulation. Among these applications, LLM-based user simulators provide a flexible way to evaluate recommender systems without relying on live user feedback. However, existing simulators typically reduce user behaviour to static preference matching based on fixed user profiles, overlooking the fact that real decisions may also reflect recent preference shifts and exploratory behaviour. To address this limitation, we propose IntRecSim (Intent-aware Recommendation Simulation), a plug-in behavioural control framework for LLM-based user simulation. IntRecSim introduces a lightweight intent mechanism that guides whether the simulated decision should follow long-term preferences, recent behavioural evidence, or exploratory behaviour. Since standard recommendation datasets lack explicit intent annotations, we construct pseudo-intent supervision from historical interactions using hybrid category and semantic preference signals. The inferred intent is injected into the LLM simulator as a dynamic control signal, making the framework compatible with different profile-generation backbones. Experiments on three benchmark datasets, covering discrimination and ranking tasks show that IntRecSim improves simulation performance in most evaluated settings. Further analysis highlights the importance of explicit behavioural control for modelling realistic user decisions in LLM-based recommender simulation.

others.title: Better Together: Human-LLM Pairs for Reliable System Rankings
others.abstract: We consider the problem of assigning two bronze (i.e. ''non-topic-creator'') assessors per topic for constructing an IR test collection, where the quality of human assessors is unknown. Given the advent of LLM-as-a-judge strategies in IR evaluation, replacing one or both of the human assessors with an LLM certainly seems appealing. But which is the best assessor pairing strategy for the purpose of obtaining an effective system ranking that represents a collective view of human assessors? To address this question, we leverage a unique existing web search test collection whose relevance assessments were contributed by a total of 24 assessors. The collection consists of non-overlapping subcollections, each with over 50 topics. For each subcollection, our target system ranking reflects the collective view of eight assessors. We then form all possible pairs from a pool of 12—comprising the original eight assessors plus four LLMs—and evaluate how well each pair's generated ranking approximates the target ranking with only two assessors. Across the three subcollections, the best performing pair type is Human-Human (H-H), but the Human-LLM (H-LLM) pair is only 0.009 Kendall's τ behind on average. Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) further show that H-LLM pairs are practically equivalent to H-H pairs under a pre-defined margin. Furthermore, H-H pairs are not uniformly strong, as human assessors have larger performance variance and can occasionally underperform H-LLM pairs when a reliable LLM is used. When Llama 4—which produced output format errors during label generation—is excluded, H-LLM pairs surpass H-H on average. Our results suggest that pairing one human with a reliable LLM can closely approximate the collective view of the eight assessors for ranking systems.

others.title: Terminal-Optimal Graph Diffusion with Null-Model-Constrained and Structure-Preserving Noise
others.abstract: Graph diffusion models have emerged as a promising approach for generating complex networks, yet they typically face two major drawbacks. First, terminating the forward process in pure Gaussian noise eliminates the intrinsic structural signatures of the original network, which leads to suboptimal generation quality. Second, the absence of constraints along the diffusion trajectory causes progressive degradation of topological features, ultimately resulting in complete structural collapse. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Null-Model-Constrained Graph Diffusion (NMC-GD), a principled framework incorporating specialized designs for graph generation. Specifically, we substitute the conventional isotropic prior with a null-model distribution as the new forward diffusion endpoint, explicitly preserving critical statistical properties of the network. In addition, we develop a null-model-guided continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) and design a directional noise term that enforces a global structural constraint on the diffusion trajectory, striking a balance between stochasticity and structural invariance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that NMC-GD achieves superior generation quality and computational efficiency.

others.title: TRACE: Tracing Temporal Constraints for Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
others.abstract: Complex temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA) requires composing multiple time-dependent facts under constraints such as validity intervals, temporal ordering, overlap, and set-style operations. Recent LLM-based approaches improve temporal reasoning through retrieval, decomposition, or planning, but the temporal constraints produced during intermediate reasoning are often left implicit: retrieved evidence may be temporally invalid, intermediate answers may be propagated without verification, and deterministic temporal operations may still be handled by free-form generation. We propose TRACE, a temporal-constraint-aware recursive framework that traces temporal constraints across retrieval, answer verification, constraint propagation, and execution. TRACE grounds temporal anchors and operators from sub-questions and intermediate answers, performs operator-aware temporal retrieval, verifies child-derived answers using grounding, bridge evidence, and operator consistency, and invokes symbolic temporal execution when root-level temporal operations are deterministically resolvable. Experiments on MultiTQ and TimelineKGQA show that TRACE improves multi-step and operator-sensitive temporal reasoning under the evaluated settings. Detailed analyses further show that verified answer propagation reduces error accumulation, while symbolic temporal execution is particularly effective for compositional temporal relations such as intersection and union. These results demonstrate that complex TKGQA benefits not only from retrieving or decomposing temporal questions, but also from explicitly tracing, verifying, and executing temporal constraints throughout the reasoning process.

others.title: Text-Conditioned Scene Graph Sequence Generation via Discrete Diffusion
others.abstract: Scene graphs represent visual scenes as objects and their relationships. While considerable research has explored predicting scene graph sequences from images or videos, generating such sequences from text remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce a discrete diffusion framework for text-conditioned scene graph sequence generation, focusing on visual scenes centered on human--object interactions. The proposed framework represents each sequence as a fixed-slot discrete state, where each slot encodes the state of an object over time, and employs a Transformer-based denoiser to generate scene graph sequences aligned with the input text. The denoiser jointly leverages within-frame slot attention, cross-frame temporal attention, and text cross-attention to capture inter-object relationships, temporal dynamics, and text--graph correspondence. We compare the proposed framework with diverse baselines, including retrieval-based methods, scene graph parsers, large language models, sequence-to-sequence models, and non-diffusion generative models. Experimental results show that our framework improves both text--graph alignment and the accuracy of temporal dynamics represented in scene graph sequences, including object appearance, persistence, and disappearance.

others.title: SEMAPHORE: Semantic Detour over Incomplete Knowledge Graphs for Multi-hop Numerical QA
others.abstract: Numerical question answering (QA) over Knowledge Graphs (KGs) requires retrieving numerical values from structured sources. Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) and KG-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) methods exploit multi-hop connectivity for entity-centric questions but remain brittle for numerical queries, whose values typically appear as sparse attribute leaves. When required triples are missing, target values can become unreachable by explicit traversal; structural methods may retrieve values from the wrong numerical attribute, while numerical solvers assuming directly attached values cannot access non-local evidence. We propose SEMAPHORE, a neuro-symbolic framework that reformulates numerical QA over KGs as a semantic detour problem. SEMAPHORE combines symbolic path planning with embedding-based geometric navigation and decoupled scoring that separates relational navigation from numerical attribute grounding. This design identifies plausible detours while preserving the metric semantics required for accurate numerical answers. On numerical QA benchmarks derived from FB15K-237 and YAGO15K, SEMAPHORE outperforms strong LLM and KG-augmented baselines, demonstrating the value of semantic detours for robust numerical knowledge access over KGs. Sparsity and cross-dataset transfer experiments show that this advantage persists under severe graph incompleteness and when target-specific Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) training is replaced with transferred schema embeddings. Code is available at https://github.com/orcies8147/SEMAPHORE.

others.title: Amplified and Emergent Safety Risks in Multi-Agent Recommendation and Retrieval
others.abstract: Recommendation and retrieval systems are increasingly built by composition, with pipelines of LLM-powered agents that retrieve, reason, and act replacing standalone models. This shift inherits long-standing risks while introducing new ones, yet the resulting threats to robustness and safety, and the strategies to contain them, remain underexplored. Focusing on multi-agent recommender systems, this tutorial organises these threats along three tiers, from drift through misalignment to compromise, and separates risks that composition merely amplifies from those that emerge only once agents interact. Because agents that each pass their own safety checks can still interact in unsafe ways, we also show how to scope evaluation to the level at which each failure surfaces: the individual agent, the interaction, or the composed system. Interactive walkthroughs of simulated attacks illustrate how these failures propagate through complete recommender and retrieval pipelines.

others.title: LLMTGL: Large Language Models for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Missing Text and Label Noise
others.abstract: Text-attributed graphs have attracted considerable attention due to their extensive applications in domains such as social networks and citation networks. Existing methods typically rely on reliable text-attributed graphs. However, the frequent occurrence of missing text in real-world scenarios severely constrains model performance. Meanwhile, label noise is inevitably introduced during the data annotation process, leading to a degradation in the performance of graph learning. The large language model (LLM), with their text generation and semantic understanding, offers a unified solution to the challenges of missing text and label noise. To jointly address both challenges, we propose LLMTGL, a novel graph learning framework for text-attributed graph node classification. Specifically, we introduce graph topological properties to construct augmented prompts that guide the LLM in generating semantically coherent academic text descriptions for nodes with missing text. Subsequently, we design an LLM-driven pseudo-label expansion mechanism that selects high-confidence unlabeled nodes to the training set. This framework jointly optimizes for missing text and label noise by integrating graph topological structure with semantic information. Experimental results demonstrate that LLMTGL achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on text-missing graphs with noisy labels. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLMTGL-EC24ssjs.

others.title: Can Frontier LLMs Capture $40 Billion in Supply Chain Value?
others.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on many NLP tasks, but their ability to reason about complex supply chain relationships remains unclear. We introduce the Supply Chain Intuition Exam (SCIE), a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can identify and infer direct and indirect supplier relationships. We compare standard LLMs, models with grounding-based retrieval, and deep research (DR) systems. Despite access to public financial reports and real-world data, recall remains low: standard and grounded models achieve approximately 3--16%, while the best DR systems reach only 22%. These results suggest that retrieval alone is insufficient for professional-grade supply chain reasoning. SCIE highlights the need for methods that better integrate domain knowledge, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning in business and finance applications.

others.title: POLAR: Policy Optimization through Larger Reasoners
others.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a practical way to improve the reasoning and decision-making abilities of large language models, but its training signal is often sparse. When a policy faces prompts beyond its current ability, every sampled trajectory in a group may fail the verifier, resulting in an all-zero group. In this case, group-relative policy optimization gives little useful gradient even when the prompt contains valuable learning content. This capacity-difficulty mismatch is especially costly for smaller models used in knowledge-intensive and web-interaction tasks. We present POLAR, a difficulty-aware training framework that augments on-policy RL with conditional guidance from a larger reasoner. POLAR uses the standard GRPO branch when at least one sampled response succeeds, and switches to a supervised objective over verified teacher trajectories only when the whole student group receives zero reward. The method can turn otherwise wasted all-zero groups into targeted learning opportunities while keeping policy exploration on prompts the student can handle. We formalize the switching criterion, teacher selection objective, mixed RL/supervised loss, and compute overhead. We evaluate POLAR on WebShop, GAIA, and WebWalkerQA using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B policies. The results show consistent gains over matched GRPO baselines, with large improvements on hard web traversal questions for the two smaller policies. Ablations and diagnostics further show that the gains come from the proposed all-zero recovery mechanism.

others.title: PRISM: Reliable LLM Knowledge Distillation from Graph-Context Perspectives for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
others.abstract: Text-attributed graph (TAG) learning aims to leverage both textual attributes and graph structures for node classification. Recent studies have utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-labels and rationales for few-label TAG learning. However, existing approaches typically rely solely on the textual attribute of target nodes, making the generated knowledge susceptible to noise and unreliability. To address this limitation, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Reliable Imitation with Semantic Multiplicity), a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework for few-label TAG learning. PRISM constructs multiple structural-context perspectives for each target node and estimates the reliability of LLM-generated knowledge based on cross-perspective consistency. The resulting reliability weights are then incorporated into the distillation process, enabling GNNs to place greater emphasis on more reliable supervision signals. Extensive experiments on five TAG benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms existing methods in few-label node classification.

others.title: Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning for LLM Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
others.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are fundamental for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in factually consistent reasoning across diverse data-mining tasks. However, when reasoning over complex graph topologies, LLMs can be brittle in maintaining structural consistency and may rely on spurious correlations. We propose SKILL (Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning), a novel paradigm that transforms relational rules from passive symbolic patterns into explicit, generation-time symbolic guidance for LLM-based reasoning. Unlike existing methods that isolate symbolic mining from neural inference, SKILL introduces a semantically aligned rule synthesis framework that filters spurious patterns and enables LLMs to leverage relational regularities during inference. By grounding generation in pruned, query-specific subgraph structures together with rule–path evidence, SKILL improves inductive generalization while preserving generative flexibility. Extensive experiments on three inductive benchmarks demonstrate that SKILL achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to a 5% absolute improvement in Hits@1, highlighting a new and effective way to integrate symbolic structure into LLM reasoning over knowledge graphs. Source code is available at https://github.com/luilui97/SKILL.

others.title: SymGRPO: Preventing Mode Collapse in Group Relative Policy Optimization via Symmetric Anti-Reinforcement
others.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become the dominant critic-free method for reinforcement learning from human feedback in large language models, with growing adoption for fine-tuning LLM-based retrievers, query reformulators, rerankers, and agentic search systems. We identify a fundamental failure mode of GRPO in multi-prompt training: prompt-blind mode collapse, where the policy converges to a single output regardless of input prompt—a critical concern for information retrieval applications where prompt-conditioned behavior is essential. We prove this arises from a quadratic gradient vanishing at the collapsed state: GRPO's entropy restoration rate is Θ(ε2|log ε|) where ε = 1 − πmax. We propose SymGRPO, which augments GRPO with an anti-reinforcement log-barrier on unchosen tokens, raising the restoration rate to Θ(ε|log ε|)—a diverging ratio of α(V − 1)/ε. Critically, this benefit appears only when the batch advantage sum S ≠ 0, which holds under EMA baselines but is forced to zero by standard mean-zero normalization. Across four small-scale reasoning tasks, GRPO mode-collapses to 19–50% accuracy while SymGRPO reaches 100% on multi-solution tasks. The modification is three lines of code.

others.title: ACMDG: An Effective and Scalable Active Clustering via Multi-granularity Diffusion Graph
others.abstract: Active clustering injects minimal human feedback into clustering via pairwise constraints, which is highly useful in data mining pipelines but difficult to scale in practice. Existing methods are expensive in two stages: initialization often requires building costly global structures, and each interaction round may trigger heavy recomputation. Meanwhile, substantial accuracy gains still demand many constraints. We present ACMDG, an effective and scalable active clustering framework built on a multi-granularity diffusion graph. ACMDG constructs a sparse yet connected multi-granularity diffusion graph structure by progressively modeling data relationships from fine-grained nearest-neighbor links to coarse-grained representations. Within an iterative refinement framework, it selects informative nodes in batch mode, categorizes them efficiently via a neighborhood-set-based interaction strategy, and refines clustering by diffusion-based label propagation. The overall framework runs in O(n log n) time. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show that ACMDG outperforms its counterparts in most cases in terms of clustering quality and scalability, while requiring significantly fewer constraints. Code is available at: https://github.com/BZhXuang/ACMDG_CIKM2026

others.title: FAIR-PIVOT: Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion for Mitigating Political Bias in Web Corpora
others.abstract: Large-scale web corpora (e.g., C4) are severely imbalanced in terms of political perspective: on the death penalty issue, e.g., left-leaning documents outnumber right-leaning ones by more than 8-fold. Such imbalances can transfer to downstream large language models, reinforcing political bias. We propose Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion (simply, FAIR-PIVOT), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based two-level-agent framework that builds balanced perspective-inverted synthetic data for politically sensitive topics. After annotating web texts with multi-persona LLMs, FAIR-PIVOT retrieves documents from contrasting orientations and inverts their viewpoint, preserving authentic discourse structure rather than rephrasing the same-view text. Across nine topics, FAIR-PIVOT generates 13,954 instances and reduces the total variation distance, a measure of how far the orientation distribution deviates from uniform balance, by up to 83%, while improving linguistic fluency as measured by Perplexity (25.5 → 21.8 ↓). Fine-tuning small language models on the balanced corpus further shifts their downstream behavior toward the intended orientation (Gemma (L--R)% +48 → +34, Qwen +55 → +50), confirming that data-level balancing can yield fairer model responses. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/bigbases/FAIR-PIVOT.

others.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Address Linkage in Tracking Ecosystems via Large Language Models
others.abstract: User tracking aims to identify network activities belonging to the same user across websites and network environments, supporting applications such as personalized recommendation and targeted advertising. As dynamic address allocation and modern privacy protections constrain traditional tracking methods, traffic-based tracking techniques have emerged to link dynamic addresses through traffic patterns. However, existing methods usually rely on large-scale user labels for supervised training, while such labels are difficult to obtain in TLS encrypted traffic, severely limiting model generalization. In this paper, we propose SLATE, a self-supervised address linkage framework integrated with LLMs under limited labeled data. Specifically, SLATE introduces a homologous subgraph discrimination task based on address behavior partitioning, which encourages the encoder to capture stable behavior patterns across temporal evolution from large-scale unlabeled data. Moreover, SLATE develops a graph semantic projection module, which enables the LLM to better interpret behavior graph representations through graph-text matching and node semantic classification, and further leverages its reasoning capability to support address linkage decisions. We evaluate SLATE on two real-world user datasets. Experimental results show that SLATE substantially outperforms the strongest self-supervised methods, achieving an average improvement of over 15% in Hits@1, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art supervised methods. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of combining self-supervised learning with LLMs for address linkage in tracking ecosystems.

others.title: Co-JDPRec: Collaborative Joint Dynamic Pruning for Efficient LLM-based Generative Recommendation
others.abstract: Generative recommendation leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to model item semantics and user preference dynamics through sequence-to-token generation, but deep Transformer layers and wide Feed Forward Network (FFN) dimensions introduce substantial memory and latency overhead in online recommendation scenarios. Existing LLM pruning methods are mainly designed to preserve general language modeling ability, often overlooking the recommendation-specific states shaped by item semantics, collaborative signals, and temporal preference dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose Co-JDPRec, a collaborative joint dynamic pruning framework that shifts the pruning objective from parameter removal to recommendation-state preservation. Specifically, Co-JDPRec introduces a task-aware saliency criterion that combines collaborative alignment and sequence-order sensitivity, enabling the model to identify neurons critical for user-item relations and evolving preference dynamics. Guided by this saliency, Co-JDPRec jointly searches FFN width and layer depth to derive a compact heterogeneous architecture, followed by distillation recovery to restore recommendation performance. Theoretically, Co-JDPRec characterizes structural importance via first-order Taylor sensitivity under recommendation-aware objectives. Empirically, it achieves superior accuracy–efficiency trade-offs on both title-based and semantic-ID-based generative recommendation backbones, validating the effectiveness of recommendation-state-aware pruning.

others.title: E²L³AE: End-to-End Text Encoder Tuning for LLM-Enhanced Linear Autoencoders
others.abstract: Enriching sparse user–item interactions with semantic item knowledge is essential for robust recommendation, particularly for long-tail items where collaborative signals are weak or unreliable. L³AE integrates frozen LLM embeddings into linear autoencoders, but fixed text representations can be suboptimal for recommendation because consumption-relevant item characteristics often deviate from general textual semantics. We propose an end-to-end extension that fine-tunes the text encoder within the same linear autoencoder framework, encouraging its embeddings to reflect item relatedness derived from user–item interactions, thereby adapting pretrained textual knowledge to recommendation objectives while remaining grounded in pretrained semantic knowledge. Experiments on public datasets show that our end-to-end trained hybrid model improves upon the original L³AE and other baselines. Moreover, the fine?tuned encoder alone serves as a competitive semantic?based recommender.

others.title: CoRe-Rec: Budgeted Consistency Policy Re-Rolling for Sequential Recommendation
others.abstract: Real-time sequential recommendation requires policies that are both expressive and efficient. Diffusion policies can model diverse user preferences, but their iterative denoising process introduces high serving latency. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) actors usually execute a single sampled action without checking whether the action is likely to trigger a positive user response before exposure. We propose CoRe-Rec, a budgeted consistency-policy re-rolling framework for RL-based slate recommendation. CoRe-Rec uses a shared consistency actor to generate continuous hyper-actions in one or few denoising steps. Each hyper-action induces a provisional slate through top-K item scoring. Before execution, a frozen user response model (URM) evaluates multiple low-cost candidates generated with different sampler configurations and noise seeds, and an early-stopping rule selects the best slate under an inference budget. The re-rolling step is a detached test-time search procedure: gradients are not propagated through the discrete sampler selection or the top-K slate construction; instead, the selected branch is recomputed for actor-critic learning. Experiments in simulated environments built from RL4RS, BookCrossing, and MovieLens 1M show that CoRe-Rec improves cumulative reward and episode depth while providing a favorable reward--latency trade-off.

others.title: Interpretation-Aware Image Manipulation Detection
others.abstract: Image manipulation has been a common practice since the early days of photography, and has evolved into a sophisticated threat with the rise of powerful image editing tools and generative AI. It can be used to spread misinformation, manipulate public opinion, and cause harm to individuals and communities. In this article, we study the problem of determining whether an image is misleading, i.e. edited in a misleading way. We introduce a risk framework to assess the intrinsic interpretive shift (ITS) of an ordered image pair, which evaluates whether the final edited image changes the interpretation supported by a source reference image. We show our risk framework can be operationalized with the Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) provenance framework. We estimate ITS with a single-call vision-language implementation of our risk framework, which first checks for meaningful visual differences, then tests whether the differences induce interpretive shift, and finally determines whether the shift is fully explained by permissible transformations rather than content-level changes. The system outputs a binary label (potentially misleading or not) together with interpretive clues and a short justification. To test the approach and show that ITS is a measurable proxy for misleading edits, we built a benchmark of 418 ordered pairs, drawn from real-world fact-check cases and meaning-preserving transformations. The best-performing model configuration (gpt-5.4) achieves 88.2% precision, 94.2% recall, and 96.5% balanced accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/liyu0x/ITS_detection/.
